learn.title: Governance structure: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and tagging
objectives: Design a shallow management group hierarchy that follows the Cloud Adoption Framework Azure landing zone model
Use subscriptions as the unit of scale, billing, policy and access, and plan for subscription limits and vending
Group resources into resource groups by shared lifecycle and apply a consistent naming convention
Design a tagging strategy with mandatory tags enforced and inherited through Azure Policy for cost allocation
Assign Azure Policy and RBAC at the highest scope that is correct, and relate EA and MCA billing hierarchies to that structure
concepts: Management group

A container above subscriptions used to apply Azure Policy and RBAC to many subscriptions at once. A tenant supports up to 10,000 management groups and six levels of depth below the root, not counting the subscription level.
Tenant root group

The top management group created for each Microsoft Entra tenant. It cannot be moved or deleted; CAF recommends creating an intermediate root group beneath it instead of assigning everything at the root.
Azure landing zone
The CAF reference architecture: a Platform management group (Identity, Management, Connectivity) plus a Landing zones group (Corp, Online), with Sandbox and Decommissioned groups alongside.
Platform landing zone
Subscriptions that host shared services such as hub networking, domain controllers and the central Log Analytics workspace, run by a central platform team.
Application landing zone
A subscription prepared for one workload or environment, placed under Corp or Online so that it inherits the right policies.
Subscription
The unit of billing, scale and isolation. Each subscription trusts exactly one Entra tenant and has its own quotas and limits, such as 980 resource groups.
Subscription vending
Automated, repeatable creation of subscriptions (for example with Bicep or Terraform and the subscription alias API) that sets the billing scope, management group placement, networking and RBAC.
Resource group
A logical container whose resources should share a lifecycle. Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group, and deleting the group deletes everything in it.
Tag
A name/value pair on a resource, resource group or subscription; up to 50 per object. Tags are not inherited by default and tag values are case-sensitive.
Modify effect
An Azure Policy effect that adds or replaces tags during create or update. Existing resources need a remediation task, which runs under a managed identity.
Cost Management tag inheritance
A billing setting for EA and MCA accounts that applies subscription and resource group tags to usage records without changing the resources themselves.
Billing hierarchy

EA uses enrollment, departments, accounts and subscriptions; MCA uses billing account, billing profiles (one invoice each), invoice sections and subscriptions. It is separate from the management group hierarchy.
comparisons: Management groups only organise governance (policy and RBAC inheritance). Subscriptions are where billing, quotas and resources actually live.
Corp holds workloads that need private connectivity to the hub and on-premises; Online holds internet-facing workloads that do not need that connectivity.
Sandbox holds experimentation subscriptions that are isolated from corporate networks. Decommissioned holds subscriptions that are being shut down, with policies that block new deployments.
Policy tag inheritance vs Cost Management tag inheritance
Azure Policy (Modify) writes the tag onto the resource itself. Cost Management tag inheritance only adds the tag to cost and usage data.
EA departments vs MCA billing profiles and invoice sections
EA departments group accounts for chargeback inside one enrollment. In MCA, a billing profile produces a separate invoice and invoice sections organise costs within that invoice.
Deny vs Modify for mandatory tags
Deny blocks resources that are missing the tag. Modify adds the tag for the user, often taking the value from the resource group or subscription.
traps: Do not build management groups per environment (dev, test, prod) or to mirror the org chart; separate environments with subscriptions and add a management group only when policy or access genuinely differs.
Tags on a resource group or subscription do not flow down to resources unless you assign an inheritance policy or turn on Cost Management tag inheritance.
A Modify or DeployIfNotExists policy affects only new or updated resources until you run a remediation task.
A resource group's location only stores metadata; its resources can be in other regions, but if that region is unavailable you cannot update those resources.
Moving a subscription to another management group immediately swaps the policies and role assignments it inherits.
Azure Blueprints is retired; use Azure Policy, template specs or deployment stacks, and infrastructure as code for subscription vending.
revision: Up to six levels of management groups below the tenant root; CAF recommends about three or four.
Each management group and subscription has exactly one parent; the root group cannot be moved or deleted.
Store custom policy definitions at the intermediate root management group so that every subscription can use them.
Use the hierarchy settings to send new subscriptions to a default management group such as Sandbox, and require permission to create management groups.
Subscriptions are the scale unit: split workloads across subscriptions before they reach quotas or limits such as 4,000 role assignments.
Group resources by lifecycle, and remember that most resources cannot be renamed, so agree on the naming convention first.
Up to 50 tags per object; values are case-sensitive; never store secrets in tags.
Use Azure Resource Graph to report tags across every subscription in the tenant.
